name: Electronic book reader
definition: A portable screen device that displays the text of books and documents stored electronically in place of paper.
what: The same Sony Data Discman DD-1 went on sale in Japan in July 1990 as an 'electronic book' player for reference works.
fit: A pocket-size battery device with its own LCD that shows the text of books and reference works stored on a 3-inch CD, replacing paper.

sources.title: Sony Data Discman
sources.quote: The DD-1 was the earlier Japanese model in 1990.

note: Replaces 1972 Yevick and Wally, for whom I found only a 1973 US patent notice (George J. Yevick, 'Mechanical optical scanner', Official Gazette 1973-05-22) and Wikipedia's unreferenced claim; a patent or concept is not a demonstration, and no working unit or contemporary report was found. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only; Bob Brown's 1930 'Readies' a proposal; Michael Hart's 1971 e-texts needed a mainframe. Sony's Data Discman DD-1 was announced May 1990 (Japan Times index) and released in Japan in July 1990; it is a commercial product, so demonstration and first practical use are the same event. Not checked: earlier Japanese dictionary/electronic-book handhelds of the 1980s (Sharp, Casio) that held a single reference text.

name: Speech recognition and voice command
definition: A machine that recognizes spoken words and carries out spoken commands, such as voice-operated doors or computers.
what: Threshold Technology (Delran/Cinnaminson, NJ) brought out the VIP-100 isolated-word recognizer and had voice-input terminals working in industrial, government and military 'real-world' use from late 1972.
fit: Spoken words were recognized by a commercial machine and used to enter data and give commands to a computer in working environments, outside the laboratory.

sources.publisher: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.title: Proceedings, 1972 Carahan Conference on Electronic Prosthetics
sources.quote: A respectable product was brought out this year by Threshold Technology, Inc.

sources.title: Real-time interactive speech technology at Threshold Technology, Incorporated
sources.quote: Threshold Technology has had voice input systems operating in these "real-world" environments since late 1972

note: Replaces the 1984 Apricot Portable. The same ERIC history says 'No commercially successful ASR device of any consequence has been developed in all these years' before Threshold's 1972 product, which supports 1972 as the first; Computerworld 1972-05-31 reports Threshold's lab demonstration of word input. Not checked: the exact first customer installation (1972-73), the earlier IBM Shoebox (1962, demonstration only) and Japanese NEC systems. A 1972 date rests on the 1977 company paper for deployment plus the contemporary product announcement.

name: Machine learning
definition: A machine that improves its performance from experience or data instead of being explicitly programmed for each task.
what: Claude Shannon at Bell Labs built Theseus, a relay-driven magnetic 'mouse' that explored a rearrangeable maze by trial and error and then ran straight to the goal on the next trial (13 s against 2 min 10 s), re-learning when the maze was changed.
fit: A machine improved its performance from experience (its relay memory of the maze it had explored) instead of being programmed with the maze.

sources.title: Shannon and his maze-solving mechanical mouse
sources.quote: The mighty mouse had remembered the maze perfectly!

sources.title: Maze for Mechanical Mouse
sources.quote: After one exploratory trial, the mouse “remembers” exactly how to proceed directly to the goal.

sources.title: Claude Shannon
sources.quote: In 1950, Shannon designed and built, with the help of his wife, Betty, a learning machine named Theseus.

note: Moves the second pass's 1951 (SNARC) back to 1950 (Theseus, built 1950; shown at the 1951 Macy cybernetics conference and in Bell Labs press in 1952). SNARC (Minsky and Edmonds, summer 1951) is later and was reported only on Wikipedia. Other candidates: Ashby's Homeostat 1948 (adapts to disturbances by random search for stability, closer to self-regulation, rejected), Grey Walter's tortoises 1948 (no learning; his conditioned-reflex version is 1951), Samuel's checkers program (1952 running, 1959 paper), Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58, Thomas Ross's 1930s maze-solving machine discussed in Psychological Review 1935 (could not read a description in the available text, so not used). Exact month of first demonstration not established.

name: Robot police and security guards
definition: Robots that patrol, guard buildings, check credentials or arrest people on behalf of authorities.
what: Denning Mobile Robotics' Sentry, marketed as an autonomous mobile security robot guard patrolling warehouses; prison units ordered by Southern Steel (600 ordered, 8 in advanced testing in late 1985).
fit: A robot that patrols facilities on its own and alerts authorities to intruders, sold to customers for real guard duty.

sources.title: Raising a new generation of robots
sources.quote: mobile se curity robot guard works in: dependently patrolling warehouses and other facilities

sources.title: Denning Sentry robot article
sources.quote: eight of these, destined for prison duty, are now undergoing ad- vanced testing

note: Replaces 2015 Knightscope: Denning Sentry (1985-86) was earlier. The exact first customer patrol deployment date was not found (1985 sources say testing/orders; Dec 1985 Robotics Age lists it as a product). Date 1986 is the earliest source describing it as working patrol service. RoboGuard/Prowler not checked.

name: Machine-readable identity and access card
definition: A card, disc or token encoded with a person's identity that machines read to grant access or check identity.
what: Line Material Industries (McGraw-Edison) used the IBM 357 data collection system in which each employee inserts his identification card at a station, the machine records who he is and his time and attendance.
fit: A machine reads each employee's ID card in daily factory use to identify him and record attendance and production against his name.

sources.title: American Machinist 1961-09-18: Vol 105 Iss 19
sources.quote: Each employee inserts his identification card in the 357 station nearest his job loca- tion

note: The ad of Sept 1961 shows a customer in use; a first use in late 1960 is likely but I found no earlier customer report. The second pass's 1968 RIT VALI-DINE (punched-hole cards admitting students to a dining hall) is later but is the earliest access-control use I found.

name: Thought-to-text and thought display
definition: A machine that writes down a person's thoughts as text, or shows their mental images or dreams on a screen.
what: Tang, LeBel, Jain and Huth (University of Texas at Austin) published a non-invasive fMRI decoder that turned brain activity into word sequences recovering the meaning of perceived speech, imagined speech (subjects imagined telling stories) and silent videos.
fit: It writes out as text, from brain activity alone, what a person is silently thinking in words, not speech they try to make; it recovers the gist rather than the exact words.

sources.publisher: Nature Neuroscience (author manuscript in PubMed Central)
sources.title: Semantic reconstruction of continuous language from non-invasive brain recordings
sources.quote: this decoder generates intelligible word sequences that recover the meaning of perceived speech, imagined speech, and even silent videos
